title: Z-RAM revived on GAA nanosheets: free floating bodies, no SOI
idea: Innovative Silicon's Z-RAM died on costly SOI wafers and a floating-body signal that shrank with scaling. Gate-all-around nanosheet stacks, already standard in logic fabs, are naturally floating bodies: write holes into 3-4 stacked sheets per cell by gate-induced drain leakage and sense the summed current shift, giving capacitorless DRAM with ~2 extra masks in any GAA foundry.
why: Deletes the capacitor module (AR 60-75 mold etch, high-k ALD, ~5-7 litho/etch steps) and the SOI premium; multi-sheet summing restores the margin that killed Z-RAM; lets U.S. GAA logic fabs build DRAM-class macros. Claimed ~30-40% fewer array process steps.

title: T-RAM rebuilt as stacked back-end oxide thyristors
idea: T-RAM's thyristor cell died needing SOI and fighting temperature-sensitive leakage in silicon. Build the p-n-p-n latch from low-temperature deposited oxides (p-type SnO or Cu2O over n-type IGZO) in back-end layers, where wide bandgaps cut thermal leakage by orders of magnitude, using one via-sized mask per tier and stacking 8 tiers above the periphery.
why: Removes SOI and front-end area; a bistable latch needs no refresh (recovers ~46 fJ/bit and 10-20% of bandwidth); 8 BEOL tiers give ~8x bits per mm2 without any EUV layer.

title: Buy bankrupt DRAM makers' patent portfolios to arm a U.S. entrant
idea: Qimonda's buried-wordline and 4F2 vertical-channel work, plus Elpida, Z-RAM, T-RAM and Kilopass portfolios, ended up with patent-assertion entities or in drawers after failure. A U.S. entrant (or a DOE-backed pool) buys or exclusively licenses them to gain freedom to operate for buried-wordline, vertical-channel and capacitorless designs on a low-EUV older node.
why: U.S. manufacturability and entry barrier: removes the litigation and royalty stack that blocks new fabs; buys ~20 years of process R&D for well under $1B, shortening time-to-first-wafer by years.

title: U.S. Memories redux: take-or-pay offtake with a price collar
idea: The 1989 U.S. Memories consortium (IBM, DEC, HP, Intel and others) collapsed before raising its ~$1B because DRAM prices fell and members refused binding purchase commitments. Fix exactly that: hyperscalers and OEMs sign 10-year take-or-pay contracts with a price collar (floor for lenders, ceiling for buyers in shortages like 2026) plus a federal buyer-of-last-resort backstop.
why: Capital intensity: investment-grade offtake cuts the fab's cost of capital from ~12% to ~6%, which on a wafer cost that is ~55% depreciation lowers cost per bit ~20-25% and makes a U.S. fab financeable.

title: DRAM bit futures exchange to end memory-cycle bankruptcies
idea: Qimonda (2009) and Elpida (2012) were killed by price troughs, not technology. Create exchange-cleared monthly futures per Gb of DDR5-equivalent bits so fabs hedge 2-3 years of output and banks lend against hedged revenue as with oil producers, while buyers hedge shortages.
why: Capital: removes the boom-bust risk premium that inflates financing and causes over/under-build; a few points lower cost of capital and steadier utilization worth ~10-15% of wafer cost.

title: Memory-only 450 mm wafers with a stripped-down tool set
idea: The G450C 450 mm program died around 2016 because toolmakers would not fund ~$20B of development against uncertain orders from three logic giants. DRAM uses far fewer distinct tool types than logic, so a memory-only 450 mm consortium with government cost share qualifies only ~40 tool types and pre-commits volume.
why: Throughput and capital per bit: 2.25x area per wafer pass; past wafer-size transitions cut cost per die ~30%; fewer, larger tools per bit lower fab capex per Gb.

title: MAPPER revived for arrays: all beamlets write one shared tile
idea: MAPPER's 13,000-beam maskless e-beam went bankrupt in 2018 because its data path (petabits per wafer) and throughput never closed. Memory arrays repeat one cell billions of times, so drive every beamlet from one shared on-chip blanking pattern broadcast to all, collapsing the data path ~1e6x, and use it only for the 3-5 array layers while periphery stays on DUV.
why: EUV dependence and mask cost: replaces EUV scanners and masks on array layers with a ~$30M maskless tool; saves ~$10M+ mask sets per node and removes the single-supplier EUV chokepoint for those layers.

title: X-ray lithography's mask killer dodged with interference-only array exposure
idea: Proximity X-ray lithography died mainly because 1x masks could not be made or inspected. DRAM arrays are periodic, so print line/space and hexagonal hole lattices by mask-free interference of 2-4 coherent EUV/soft X-ray beams split from one compact free-electron-laser source feeding 10+ exposure stations, trimmed by cheap DUV cut masks.
why: Removes EUV scanners from ~4 of the 5-7 EUV layers; one source amortized over many stations and huge depth of focus cut cost per array layer several-fold.

title: Directed self-assembly confined to DRAM's honeycomb capacitor array
idea: Directed self-assembly was abandoned for logic because defect density stalled and logic layouts are not periodic. DRAM's storage-node array is a hexagonal lattice, the native pattern of cylinder-forming block copolymers, so DUV-printed guide trenches (graphoepitaxy) multiply hole density 4-7x and residual defects are absorbed by existing row/column redundancy.
why: Replaces 1-2 EUV exposures with a ~$1M coat/anneal track; cost per patterned layer down ~5x; defect spec relaxed from logic-grade to repairable-grade.

title: IBM eDRAM trench sold as merchant pre-capacitored substrate wafers
idea: IBM's deep-trench eDRAM died when its single in-house SOI process ended with GlobalFoundries' 7 nm exit. Disaggregate it: a substrate vendor (Soitec-style) mass-produces blank wafers with a uniform grid of deep-trench capacitors, and any fab, including U.S. legacy logic fabs, builds access transistors and periphery on top aligned to that grid.
why: Capital: moves the deepest etch and high-k module into one specialized high-throughput substrate fab; lets non-memory fabs make DRAM-class memory; ~30% of DRAM process steps outsourced to a shared, fully utilized line.

title: ZettaCore redox molecules turn squat capacitors into full-charge cells
idea: ZettaCore's porphyrin molecular memory folded around 2008 because the molecules could not survive 400 C back-end steps and needed all-new circuits. Use them only as a charge multiplier: graft a redox monolayer (~1e14 molecules/cm2, ~160 fC/um2) onto the storage-node electrode after all hot steps, so an AR~8 cylinder stores the ~2.5 fC an AR~70 cylinder holds today.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and deletes the hardest high-AR mold etch and its tool fleet; capacitor-module tool hours fall ~5-10x.

title: ThruChip inductive coupling replaces HBM's through-silicon via tax
idea: Keio's ThruChip Interface (inductive coils in standard metal layers) never displaced TSVs because coil area and link power looked worse at 2010 bandwidths. Put 30-50 um coils in the DRAM top metal under each channel, thin dies to ~20 um, stack with adhesive only and bring power through edge wirebonds, so no via etch, fill, reveal or keep-out zones remain.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): removes ~10+ TSV process steps, keep-out area and much stacking yield loss; claims ~1.5-2x more stacked bits per wafer.

title: Anamartic's wafer-scale memory returns as uncut DRAM wafer blades
idea: Anamartic's 'Catt spiral' wafer-scale memory shipped in 1989 but died on weak 1980s yields and cheap boards. Today's dies carry redundancy, so skip dicing, known-good-die test and packaging: one redistribution layer daisy-chains good dies via a self-configuring spiral bus mapped at wafer test, and whole 300 mm wafers (~2 TB) mount as AI-rack memory blades.
why: Removes dicing, packaging, substrates and per-die final test (~10-20% of DRAM cost) and sidesteps the advanced-packaging capacity bottleneck.

title: MRAM's etch killer bypassed with ion-implant-defined magnetic junctions
idea: Everspin-era MRAM density and cost were throttled by etching magnetic stacks (non-volatile byproducts, sidewall redeposition, slow ion-beam etch). Deposit the MTJ stack blanket and define cells by implanting light ions (He+ or N+) through a hard mask to magnetically deaden the free layer between bits, leaving a planar, etch-free film.
why: Removes the ion-beam-etch throughput bottleneck and redeposition shorts; planar result is stackable; claims ~2-3x tool throughput and higher yield for DRAM-class-latency, unlimited-endurance cells.

title: Canon ELTRAN porous-silicon transfer builds 30-tier single-crystal 3D DRAM
idea: Canon's ELTRAN layer transfer (epitaxy on porous Si, split by water jet) lost to Smart Cut on cost for single SOI layers. For 3D DRAM needing 26+ single-crystal tiers its advantage returns: one donor is re-epitaxied and split repeatedly, each tier bonded below 400 C onto the growing stack with one coarse alignment litho per tier and no hydrogen implant.
why: No manufacturable 3D cell (fact 2): supplies single-crystal lateral-transistor tiers without Si/SiGe superlattice limits; donor reused ~50x; per-tier cost ~one bond plus split.

title: Fill Optane's empty fab: a toll memory foundry for fabless DRAM
idea: Optane died partly because Intel alone could not fill the Lehi fab, so fixed costs crushed unit cost. Create a memory toll foundry with an open DRAM PDK (cell, sense-amp and redundancy libraries) so AI-chip firms and hyperscalers tape out custom DRAM dies and share one fab's utilization.
why: Capital: >90% utilization across many products instead of one product's swings; amortizes a U.S. fab over many customers; custom dies cut overfetch and periphery waste.

title: Ball Semiconductor's sealed-flow, cleanroom-free fab applied to flat memory wafers
idea: Ball Semiconductor proposed processing 1 mm silicon spheres in sealed tubes without a cleanroom and failed because lithography on spheres was poor. Keep the part that worked, sealed continuously flowing minienvironments, but carry flat wafers in nitrogen-purged pods through linked single-wafer modules so DRAM's repetitive flow needs no ballroom cleanroom.
why: Fab cost: cleanroom shell and HVAC are ~20-30% of capex and much of a fab's water and energy; claims ~25% capex cut and an 18-month build.

title: Cavendish Kinetics' stiction problem inverted into a refresh-free NEMS bit
idea: Cavendish Kinetics' MEMS memory fought stiction and pivoted away. Make stiction the storage: back-end nano-cantilevers latch by van der Waals force onto a contact (1) or rest open (0) and are released by a pull-off electrode, and the electromechanical hysteresis window rejects half-selected cells so a passive crossbar needs no transistor.
why: Refresh-free with zero standby leakage (fact 3); metal-and-dielectric-only BEOL process at ~3 masks per deck, stackable over periphery, no front-end area.

title: Wafer-level burn-in revived as contactless, self-powered on-wafer BIST
idea: Early wafer-level burn-in for DRAM failed on the cost and planarity of full-wafer probe contactors. Build a scribe-line power grid fed by two large pads per wafer; every die runs on-chip BIST and burn-in in a heated cassette, burns results into fuses and reports through an on-die photodiode/LED or near-field link.
why: Throughput and capex: removes probe cards and most ATE time from memory test, a large share of back-end capital; claims ~50-70% test-capex cut.

title: Qimonda's trench DRAM resurrected by metal-assisted chemical etching
idea: Infineon/Qimonda's trench DRAM lost to stacked capacitors around 2009 because plasma etching of silicon trenches beyond ~AR 70 became impossible. Metal-assisted chemical etching (a catalyst mesh sinking into Si in HF/H2O2) reaches AR >100 in a room-temperature wet bench, so sink buried capacitors before the transistors using a self-aligned, non-gold catalyst grid stripped before gate oxidation.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): AR 115+ via wet chemistry instead of $10M+ etch tools; capacitor-module capex down ~10x.

title: Fab helium recapture loops, fixing why 1990s recovery was abandoned
idea: Earlier fab helium-recovery efforts were abandoned once helium got cheap. With Qatar offline, add membrane/cryogenic recapture skids on every etch and CVD tool's backside-cooling and purge lines with a site liquefier, switch non-critical purges to argon, and use contracts that reward recaptured volume.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar ~30% offline): 80-90% recovery cuts fab helium purchases ~5-10x and protects output from supply shocks.

title: Continuous Czochralski growth stretches each Spruce Pine quartz crucible
idea: Continuous Czochralski (CCZ) was tried in the 1980s-90s and dropped as batch CZ improved. Feed polysilicon granules continuously into a double crucible so one high-purity quartz crucible grows 5-8 DRAM-grade 300 mm ingots instead of one, with steadier oxygen content for retention uniformity.
why: Spruce Pine (>80%) crucible chokepoint: quartz per wafer down 5-8x; slight retention-tail improvement from uniform oxygen.

title: Pay memory subsidies per gigabyte shipped, not per fab dollar
idea: Capex-first support such as Solyndra's loan guarantee failed by funding plants that never reached competitive cost. Restructure U.S. memory support as a production tax credit per Gb of DRAM-class memory shipped from U.S. fabs, decaying over 10 years, with a bonus per Gb made without EUV layers.
why: Capital efficiency and U.S. manufacturability: money flows to whoever reaches volume and low cost, rewards low-EUV processes, and grows U.S. share from 1-2%.

title: IBM racetrack grown in anodized-alumina pores with zero bit-scale lithography
idea: IBM's racetrack memory died because nobody could fabricate its vertical 3D magnetic nanowires. Anodize aluminium into self-ordered 30-60 nm pores tens of um deep, pulse-electroplate Co/Ni-Cu modulated nanowires whose composition steps act as domain-wall pinning notches (~100 bits per wire), and read pore clusters holding majority-voted copies through a coarse MTJ crossbar underneath.
why: Meets 100x: no lithography at bit scale, only anodizing and plating baths, ~100 bits stacked per pore; est. <$0.05/GB vs ~$5-10/GB DRAM. Trades: 50-500 ns shift latency and sequential bias (good for streaming AI weights), redundancy overhead.

title: 3D XPoint rebuilt vertically: one hole mask for 200 layers
idea: 3D XPoint died on cost: every deck needed its own critical patterning and tall double etch, so two decks never undercut DRAM enough. Use the 3D NAND recipe instead: stack 200 metal/oxide word planes, drill one hole array, line holes with a self-selecting chalcogenide film and fill with a metal bitline pillar, so every plane-pillar crossing is a cell made with the same single critical mask.
why: Meets 100x: litho amortized over 200 layers like NAND, est. ~$0.05-0.1/GB. Trades: ~1e8-1e9 endurance (wear-leveled behind a small DRAM cache), us-class writes, thermal disturb between planes.

title: Nanoimprint's overlay killer neutralized by alignment-free stacked crossbars
idea: Canon's nanoimprint for NAND stalled on overlay error and defects. Perpendicular line arrays need no overlay because every crossing is a cell wherever lines land, so imprint 15 nm half-pitch lines from daughter templates replicated off one e-beam master, stack 16 decks of amorphous-carbon sp2/sp3 switching cells with shared lines, and absorb random offsets with a per-array line calibration map.
why: Meets 100x: no EUV, imprint tools ~1/5 scanner cost, 16 decks of 4F2 cells; est. ~$0.05-0.1/GB. Trades: carbon-cell endurance and write energy, template wear, defect mapping.

title: Self-assembly's defect killer made irrelevant by cell-level defect maps
idea: Directed self-assembly never met logic defect specs (<0.01/cm2). Accept raw lamellar block-copolymer line arrays with ~1% bad crossings; after fab a controller sweep writes a compressed per-array defect bitmap, and the memory controller skips bad sites through Bloom-filter lookups so the media never needs to be perfect.
why: Meets 100x: sub-10 nm lines from a coat/bake track with no EUV or imprint, stacked 16+ decks; est. <$0.1/GB. Trades: ~3% spare capacity, lookup latency, mapping time at test.

title: GE's BEAMOS reborn: microcolumn electron beams address unpatterned MOS film
idea: GE's 1970s beam-addressed MOS memory (BEAMOS) wrote and read charge on a MOS target with an electron beam, but died on bulky vacuum tubes and slow deflection. Wafer-fabricate 10,000 MEMS microcolumns in a chip-scale vacuum package, each deflecting a 10-20 nm spot across a 100 um field of an unpatterned SiO2/Si target and reading bits by beam-induced current.
why: Meets 100x: the storage medium needs zero lithography and each column covers ~25 Mb; est. $0.02-0.1/GB. Trades: vacuum packaging, ~100 ns-1 us access, beam-induced oxide wear limits endurance unless run at low voltage.

title: Thinfilm's printed ferroelectric memory scaled by roll-to-roll nanoimprint
idea: Thin Film Electronics' printed P(VDF-TrFE) memory topped out at ~20-36 bits per label because it was screen-printed at ~100 um. Keep the cheap polymer and the roll-to-roll web but pattern crossbars on metallized PET by roll nanoimprint at 50 nm, then laminate 20 sheets into a block wired at its edge to a CMOS controller.
why: Meets 100x: R2R capital per m2 is ~1/1000 of a wafer fab and 50 nm 4F2 gives ~12 TB per m2 per layer; est. <$0.05/GB. Trades: us switching, 1e6-1e8 endurance, bulky form factor.

title: Plated-wire memory reborn as thermally drawn crossbar ribbons
idea: Plated-wire memory (UNIVAC, 1960s-70s) died because hand-made wires could not reach semiconductor density. Thermally draw a preform of parallel metal electrodes embedded in a phase-change chalcogenide glass cladding down ~1000x into ribbons with ~200 nm electrode pitch, then laminate ribbons at 90 degrees so every electrode crossing becomes a cell, 50 laminations deep.
why: Meets 100x: patterning by a ~$5M drawing tower producing km per hour instead of lithography; est. ~$0.05/GB. Trades: coarse pitch, ribbon-registration yield, PCM endurance and write energy.

title: Josephson-era missing memory: 77 K thin-oxide 3D NAND as DRAM
idea: IBM's Josephson program (cancelled 1983) and later cryogenic computing stalled for lack of dense, cheap cold memory. At 77 K leakage collapses, so a 3D NAND-style vertical string with a 1.5-2 nm direct-tunneling oxide instead of ~7 nm Fowler-Nordheim oxide programs at ~3-5 V in tens of ns, suffers little hot-carrier wear and holds charge for hours.
why: Meets 100x: NAND cost structure (~$0.03-0.08/GB) with near-DRAM write speed, refresh-free hours retention and ~1e12-class endurance. Trade: liquid-nitrogen cooling (~10-15% facility overhead).

title: SEL's IGZO DOSRAM built on glass in shuttered LCD fabs
idea: Semiconductor Energy Laboratory's IGZO DOSRAM never found a fab, while Gen-8 to Gen-10 LCD fabs such as Sharp Sakai are closing. Retool one closed line with roll-to-plate nanoimprint at 30 nm, stack 4 layers of IGZO 2T0C gain cells on 2.2x2.5 m glass with wide landing pads that absorb glass distortion, and bond CMOS periphery chiplets along the panel edge.
why: Meets 100x: panel capex per m2 is ~1/100-1/500 of wafer fabs and already written off; est. ~$0.05-0.1/GB. Trades: low IGZO mobility (100 ns+ access), slab form factor, panel-scale imprint yield.

title: Audio-RAM trick revived: sell fail-bin DRAM behind remapping controllers
idea: In the 1980s, partially defective DRAMs were sold cheaply as 'audio RAM' until digital systems demanded perfect parts. Revive it for computing: fail-bin dies (bad rows, weak-retention cells, HBM stacks with one dead die) ship with a full fault map in SPD flash, a CXL controller remaps bad rows per page, and retention-weak parts run chilled to 0 C or at 32 ms refresh.
why: Meets 100x for its slice: dies otherwise scrapped (~10-20% of DRAM output, 20-30% of HBM) sell near scrap value, ~$0.05-0.1/GB. Trades: supply limited to a few % of bits, controller complexity, slightly higher refresh power.

title: 1970s CCD memory flipped vertical inside a 3D NAND stack
idea: CCD memories (Intel 2416, Fairchild) died because serial shifting lost to DRAM's random access. Turn a 3D NAND stack into vertical CCD shift registers: 2-phase clock its 300 word-line layers to push 4-level charge packets along an IGZO channel whose low generation current preserves packets for seconds, with one sense amp per string top and no storage transistor or capacitor per bit.
why: Meets 100x: NAND fab cost structure with no per-bit device, 2 bits per packet; est. ~$0.05-0.1/GB. Trades: ~150 ns average shift latency for random words, best for streamed AI weights and KV pages.

title: HP memristor's forming and selector killers fixed in a depreciated fab
idea: HP Labs' TiO2 memristor (The Machine) died on per-cell electroforming, variability and a separate selector, with no fab partner after the SK hynix deal lapsed. Use a self-rectifying Ta2O5/TaOx bilayer with a built-in series-resistor film so each deck is formed by one global flood pulse, and build 32 decks at 40 nm with dry 193 nm litho, 2 bits/cell, in a fully depreciated 300 mm fab.
why: Meets 100x: no depreciation load (55% of normal wafer cost), no EUV, 32 decks x 2 bits; est. ~$0.1/GB. Trades: ~1e9 endurance needing wear-leveling, ~100 ns reads and us writes.

title: Robotic second-life harvest of retired DRAM into CXL memory shelves
idea: DRAM reclaim from retired servers and phones has failed on manual handling, mixed generations and test cost. Decommissioning lines at hyperscalers use robots to pull DIMMs and reflow-desolder LPDDR packages, run a 10-minute BIST sort, and mount mixed DDR3/DDR4/LPDDR parts behind CXL controllers that hide generation differences in pooled second-life shelves.
why: Meets 100x: the bits are already paid for; harvest plus test ~$0.05-0.1/GB vs ~$5-10/GB new, with zero fab capex. Trades: older speeds, higher power per bit, supply tied to retirement cycles.

title: Optical-disc molding lines make spiral-crossbar memory discs
idea: The optical-disc industry collapsed under streaming, idling injection-molding lines that replicate ~100 nm grooves into a disc every ~3 seconds for cents. Mold one disc with clockwise and one with counter-clockwise sub-one-turn spiral grooves, metallize and polish them, and laminate the discs around a threshold-switching memory film so each pair of spirals crosses exactly once, with both line families reaching a CMOS hub chip bonded at the center.
why: Meets 100x: ~200,000 lines per family gives ~4e10 cells per disc pair for well under $1 of patterning, est. ~$0.05-0.1/GB with 2 bits/cell. Trades: density falls with radius, odd geometry, slow switching film.

title: Matrix Semiconductor's 3D antifuse stack made rewritable with selector-charged capacitors
idea: Matrix Semiconductor's 3D poly-diode antifuse memory (bought by SanDisk in 2005) stacked cheaply at ~4 masks per layer but died for being write-once. Keep the stacked poly pillar process and swap the antifuse for a small planar MIM capacitor charged through a bidirectional punch-through n-p-n selector, giving 1S1C dynamic cells with unlimited endurance, refreshed like DRAM.
why: Meets 100x: no access transistor, no high-AR capacitor, 8-16 DUV decks; est. ~$0.1/GB. Trades: selector leakage forces ms-scale refresh, higher refresh power, thin sense margin.

title: Z-NAND's failure fixed: erase-free 64-byte sub-page flash over CXL
idea: Samsung Z-NAND and Kioxia XL-Flash failed to win DRAM sockets because 4 KB pages and block erases left them neither cheap nor fast enough. Build an SLC die with 512-byte mini-page sense amps per plane, append 64 B cachelines as log writes into pre-erased blocks, erase in idle planes, and absorb rewrites in a 1% DRAM front, exposed as CXL.mem.
why: Meets ~50-100x: ~$0.1-0.15/GB SLC-class cost serving warm DRAM data. Trades: 1-3 us misses, ~1e5 SLC endurance hidden by the DRAM front and wear-leveling.

title: Kovio's liquid-silicon ink printed into 32 cheap gain-cell tiers
idea: Kovio printed silicon RFID from liquid cyclopentasilane and folded in 2014 on a tiny market and hard-to-handle pyrophoric ink. Inside a sealed inert coater module, spin 20 nm silicon films from ink, crystallize only the top film with a nanosecond laser, and stack 32 tiers of poly-Si 2T gain cells, each tier patterned by one imprint.
why: Meets 100x: each tier costs a spin, a laser scan and one imprint (~$5-10/wafer) instead of epitaxy or transfer; est. ~$0.1/GB. Trades: grain-boundary leakage forces ms refresh and defect mapping.

title: Mask ROM's per-design killer fixed: imprinted ROM for frozen AI weights
idea: Mask ROM died because every code change needed new masks and weeks of lead time. Frozen AI model weights are read every token but almost never rewritten, so store them in 16-deck 3D diode-ROM where every layer is a common template except one via layer per model, imprinted from a template e-beam-cut in a day, with 2 bits/cell coded by via size.
why: Meets 100x: no capacitor, no refresh, a single custom layer; est. ~$0.01-0.05/GB with low read energy. Trade: immutable, so a new model needs new dies and KV-cache still uses DRAM.

title: Hitachi's single-electron grain memory stacked in 64 cheap tiers
idea: Hitachi's room-temperature single-electron memory (Yano, 1990s) stored a few electrons in grains of 3-4 nm polysilicon and died because random grains caused wild threshold scatter. Tame the scatter with per-cell write-verify calibration and a 3-cell majority code, and exploit its simplicity of thin films with no capacitor or deep etch by depositing 64 tiers gated by one shared vertical-gate hole pattern.
why: Meets 100x: tiers are just thin depositions, writes are fast direct tunneling (~10s of ns), retention minutes to hours; est. ~$0.1/GB. Trades: 3x cell redundancy, calibration time, variability.

title: Core memory reborn as colloidally patterned magnetic vortex nanorings
idea: Ferrite core memory died because cores were hand-threaded and millimetre-sized, yet its coincident-current selection made a passive crossbar with no sneak paths. Pattern magnetic vortex nanorings with mask-free nanosphere lithography (a self-assembled bead monolayer) over a coarse X/Y/sense line grid, so only rings under full coincident field switch and several rings per crossing vote.
why: Meets 100x: no transistor per bit, litho-free ring formation, unlimited magnetic endurance and non-volatility; est. ~$0.1/GB at 8 decks. Trades: destructive read-and-restore like core, high write currents, small inductive read signal.

title: Nanosolar's non-vacuum dream fixed for memory: an atmospheric-pressure fab
idea: Nanosolar and spatial-ALD solar startups died because non-vacuum films lost on efficiency to cheap crystalline silicon. Memory arrays do not need photovoltaic-grade films, so build a fab with no vacuum chambers: damascene electroplated lines, spin-on and atmospheric spatial-ALD dielectrics, anodized memory oxide, imprint patterning, and only periphery chiplets bought from a conventional fab.
why: Meets 100x with stacked decks: vacuum PVD/CVD/etch is ~40% of fab capex and atmospheric tools are ~5-10x cheaper and faster; est. ~$0.1/GB. Trades: film quality, defect density, coarser features.

title: IBM Millipede's tip-wear killer removed by non-contact charge-writing probes
idea: IBM's Millipede thermomechanical probe storage died on tip wear, slow thermal writes and cheap flash. Hover a million-tip MEMS array ~5 nm above an unpatterned ferroelectric film, write bits by polarization-switching voltage pulses with no contact or heat, and read each bit by piezoresponse through per-tip front-ends.
why: Meets 100x: medium cost ~0 and MEMS made at ~1 um litho; est. ~$0.05/GB. Trades: us-ms seek, mechanical scanner and shock sensitivity, so it serves as a bulk tier behind DRAM.

title: Bubble memory without garnet: field-driven skyrmion loops on glass
idea: Magnetic bubble memory (Intel Magnetics, TI) died on costly gadolinium gallium garnet substrates, bias magnets and slow propagation. Sputter Pt/Co/Ta skyrmion multilayers on glass or Si, keep bubble memory's global rotating in-plane field from a package coil to move every bit at once with no per-track drivers, and define tracks with one coarse imprint and one shared magnetoresistive sensor per major loop.
why: Meets 100x: no garnet and no per-bit transistor, just a film plus one pattern; est. ~$0.05-0.1/GB. Trades: us-level serial access, coil power.
